svg.title: The Layer 2 attack chain in six stages, each with the control that cuts that link
svg.desc: A six-row table following the attacker from an unmanaged wall port to control of a server on the same subnet. One, physical access: plug in a cable or a switch, defeated by disabling unused ports, port security and 802.1X. Two, topology reconnaissance via CDP, LLDP, BPDU and DTP, defeated by turning those protocols off on access-facing ports. Three, VLAN bypass by double tagging or DTP negotiation, defeated by disabling DTP and moving the native VLAN. Four, root bridge takeover with low-priority BPDUs, defeated by BPDU Guard and Root Guard. Five, man in the middle via ARP, DHCP or IPv6 RA spoofing, defeated by DAI, DHCP snooping and RA Guard. Six, lateral spread by scanning and exploiting peers, defeated by private VLAN, SGT and host protection. A sidebar stresses that every link can be cut independently and cheaply, while an untouched chain takes about ten minutes from cable to server, so the design question is which links you are willing to leave open.
svg.text: The Layer 2 attack chain: six links, six independent chances to cut it
Nothing here needs an exploit. The chain is built from the protocols the access layer runs by default
plug a cable, or a switch of your own
the only stage that is also a physical-security answer
no CDP/LLDP on access-facing ports · no DTP
what the attacker cannot enumerate, they must guess
double tagging, or negotiate a trunk
never a trunk to an access port, ever
BPDU Guard on edge · Root Guard downstream
one err-disables the port, the other keeps it root-inconsistent
ARP spoof · DHCP spoof · IPv6 RA
DAI · DHCP snooping · IPv6 RA Guard
all three depend on a binding table - see the IP Source Guard figure
scan peers, exploit an old service
the only stage where the control is architectural, not a command
Every link is cheap to cut, and they are independent
Cutting one link forces the attacker to use a louder stage.
802.1X alone turns stage ① into a credential problem; BPDU
Guard alone makes stage ④ fail loudly in the log. You do not
need all six to be perfect - you need to know which are open.
About ten minutes from wall port to a server on the same subnet
The design question is not "do we enable everything" but "which of these six
links do we knowingly leave open, and who accepted that risk". Those answers
belong in the design document, not in the switch configuration.
Note the coupling: stages ⑤ and ⑥ depend on the same binding and segmentation data that stages ①-④ produce - one clean inventory serves all of them.
